marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q001.takeaway: Internal intercostals assist active expiration by depressing the ribs when forceful breathing against resistance is required.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q001.displayText:
Internal intercostals assist active expiration by depressing the ribs when forceful breathing against resistance is required.

The internal intercostal muscles are the muscles of expiration.

The device shown in the image is an incentive spirometer. It is a device used to help your lungs recover after surgery or a lung illness.
emphasis: Internal intercostals assist active expiration by depressing the ribs when forceful breathing against resistance is required

rationales.a: External intercostals elevate ribs during inspiration.
rationales.b: The diaphragm is the primary inspiratory muscle, not an expiratory muscle.
rationales.d: Rhomboids stabilize/retract the scapula and are not forced-expiration muscles.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q002.takeaway: Latissimus dorsi can assist forced expiration and cough; scalenes and serratus muscles can assist inspiration.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q002.displayText:
Latissimus dorsi can assist forced expiration and cough; scalenes and serratus muscles can assist inspiration.

Latissimus dorsi is not an accessory muscle of inspiration. It is an accessory muscle of expiration.

Accessory muscles of inspiration: sternocleidomastoid; scalene muscles; serratus posterior and anterior; erector spinae; pectoralis major and minor.

Breathing involves changing the thoracic volume by altering the vertical, transverse, and anteroposterior dimensions of the thorax. The diaphragm is the key muscle in respiration.

Serratus posterior superior elevates the ribs, hence aiding in inspiration. Serratus posterior inferior depresses the ribs. It is a muscle aiding in expiration.
emphasis: Latissimus dorsi can assist forced expiration and cough; scalenes and serratus muscles can assist inspiration

rationales.a: Serratus anterior can elevate ribs when the scapula is fixed.
rationales.b: Serratus posterior superior elevates ribs and assists inspiration.
rationales.d: Scalenes elevate the first two ribs during inspiratory effort.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q003.takeaway: Serratus posterior inferior depresses the lower ribs; serratus posterior superior and levatores costarum elevate ribs.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q003.displayText:
Serratus posterior inferior depresses the lower ribs; serratus posterior superior and levatores costarum elevate ribs.

Serratus posterior inferior does not elevate the ribs.

The muscles of inspiration help increase the diameters of the thoracic cavity by elevating the ribs. Serratus posterior inferior is an accessory muscle of expiration. The muscles of expiration help in the depression of the ribs.

Mnemonic: SIT-Q depressors that work along with anterior abdominals for expiration: Serratus posterior inferior; Internal intercostals; Transversus thoracis; Quadratus lumborum.
emphasis: Serratus posterior inferior depresses the lower ribs; serratus posterior superior and levatores costarum elevate ribs

rationales.c: External intercostals elevate ribs during inspiration.
rationales.d: Levatores costarum elevate ribs and assist inspiration.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q004.takeaway: The trachea begins near C6 at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, a useful level when assessing cervical injury.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q004.displayText:
The trachea begins near C6 at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, a useful level when assessing cervical injury.

The trachea starts at the level of the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage at the level of the C6 vertebra.
emphasis: The trachea begins near C6 at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, a useful level when assessing cervical injury

rationales.a: C4 is above the usual tracheal origin.
rationales.b: C5 remains above the cricoid/tracheal transition.
rationales.d: C7 is below the tracheal beginning and is not the first level to inspect.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q005.takeaway: The trachea usually bifurcates at the sternal angle around T4–T5.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q005.displayText:
The trachea usually bifurcates at the sternal angle around T4–T5.

The trachea bifurcates at the lower border of T4 vertebra.

The trachea is 10 - 12 cm long and has 2 parts: Upper cervical; Thoracic (in superior mediastinum).

Note: Although Gray's Anatomy 41st Ed states that the tracheal bifurcation is at T6, we choose to stick with T4 as multiple other textbooks give the answer as T4.
emphasis: The trachea usually bifurcates at the sternal angle around T4–T5

rationales.a: T7 is too low for the carina.
rationales.b: T6 is below the usual bifurcation level.
rationales.c: T5 is near the level, but the conventional landmark is T4/T4–T5.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q006.takeaway: The left main bronchus crosses the esophagus around 28 cm from the upper incisors.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q006.displayText:
The left main bronchus crosses the esophagus around 28 cm from the upper incisors.

The left bronchus crosses the esophagus at 28 cm from the upper incisor teeth.

Normally esophagus shows 4 constrictions at the following levels measured from upper incisors: junction of the esophagus with cricopharynx (15 cm from the incisor teeth); crossed by arch of aorta (23 cm from the incisor teeth); crossed by left bronchus (28 cm from the incisor teeth); it pierces the diaphragm (40 cm from the incisor teeth).
emphasis: The left main bronchus crosses the esophagus around 28 cm from the upper incisors

rationales.a: 23 cm from upper incisors is more proximal than the bronchial crossing level.
rationales.b: 15 cm is at the upper esophagus, far above the crossing.
rationales.c: The source measures distance from upper incisors, not lower incisors.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q007.takeaway: At the midaxillary line the pleural reflection reaches about the tenth rib; thoracentesis should not be inserted below that level.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q007.displayText:
At the midaxillary line the pleural reflection reaches about the tenth rib; thoracentesis should not be inserted below that level.

The inferior margin of the pleura in the midaxillary line is at the level of the 10th rib. So, while doing thoracentesis you would not go below this level. It is done in the 8th or 9th intercostal space so as not to damage the surrounding structures.
emphasis: At the midaxillary line the pleural reflection reaches about the tenth rib; thoracentesis should not be inserted below that level

rationales.a: Sixth rib is above the usual pleural reflection and is unnecessarily high.
rationales.c: Eighth rib is still above the pleural reflection at the midaxillary line.
rationales.d: Twelfth rib is below the safe level and would risk abdominal structures.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q008.takeaway: The oblique fissure surface line crosses the fifth rib at the midaxillary line and reaches the sixth intercostal space anteriorly, not the fourth costal cartilage.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q008.displayText:
The oblique fissure surface line crosses the fifth rib at the midaxillary line and reaches the sixth intercostal space anteriorly, not the fourth costal cartilage.

The surface marking of the oblique fissure of the lung will not touch 4th costal cartilage.

On either side, the upper and lower lobes of the lung are separated by the oblique fissure.

This can be marked by a line that runs anteroinferiorly from the posterior end of the 4th rib (the spinous process of the T3 vertebra), crosses the 5th rib in the midaxillary line, continues inferiorly, crossing either the 6th intercostal space/7th rib on the right or the 5th rib/5th intercostal space on the left, on both sides at the midclavicular line.

The left oblique fissure is located at a higher level and courses more vertically than the right oblique fissure.
emphasis: The oblique fissure surface line crosses the fifth rib at the midaxillary line and reaches the sixth intercostal space anteriorly, not the fourth costal cartilage

rationales.a: The fissure line crosses the sixth intercostal space anteriorly.
rationales.b: It crosses the fifth rib in the midaxillary line.
rationales.c: It crosses the seventh rib on the right near the midclavicular line.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q009.takeaway: In the midclavicular line the lung extends to the sixth rib; a wound below that level may spare lung tissue.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q009.displayText:
In the midclavicular line the lung extends to the sixth rib; a wound below that level may spare lung tissue.

The lower border of the lung in the midclavicular line is at the level of the 6th rib. Hence, if the entry wound is below this level, the lung is probably not injured.
emphasis: In the midclavicular line the lung extends to the sixth rib; a wound below that level may spare lung tissue

rationales.a: The twelfth rib is far below the lung border and not the threshold asked.
rationales.b: The tenth rib is also below the lung edge but a lower level than the standard sixth-rib landmark.
rationales.c: The eighth rib is below much of the lung but the stated surface level is the sixth rib.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q010.takeaway: The pleural cupola is the cervical extension of parietal pleura projecting above the first rib into the root of the neck.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q010.displayText:
The pleural cupola is the cervical extension of parietal pleura projecting above the first rib into the root of the neck.

The dome-shaped layer of parietal pleura lining the cervical extension of the pleural cavity is called cervical pleura/pleural cupola/dome of pleura.
emphasis: The pleural cupola is the cervical extension of parietal pleura projecting above the first rib into the root of the neck

rationales.a: Costal pleura lines the inner thoracic wall below the cupola.
rationales.b: Mediastinal pleura covers lateral mediastinal structures.
rationales.c: Visceral pleura directly covers the lung and does not form the cervical parietal cupola.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q011.takeaway: Mediastinal pleura is supplied by phrenic nerve sensory fibers, so irritation can refer pain to the side of the neck/shoulder.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q011.displayText:
Mediastinal pleura is supplied by phrenic nerve sensory fibers, so irritation can refer pain to the side of the neck/shoulder.

The pain from mediastinal pleura is referred to the side of the neck.
emphasis: Mediastinal pleura is supplied by phrenic nerve sensory fibers, so irritation can refer pain to the side of the neck/shoulder

rationales.b: Costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves and refers pain to thoracic wall.
rationales.c: Arm pain can occur with diaphragmatic/central pleural irritation but is not the expected mediastinal pleural referral here.
rationales.d: Abdominal wall is not the characteristic phrenic-nerve referral zone.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q012.takeaway: The right lung’s mediastinal surface is related to the superior vena cava and right atrium.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q012.displayText:
The right lung’s mediastinal surface is related to the superior vena cava and right atrium.

Superior vena cava is related to the mediastinal part of the right lung.
emphasis: The right lung’s mediastinal surface is related to the superior vena cava and right atrium

rationales.a: Arch of aorta is a prominent relation to the left lung mediastinal surface.
rationales.c: Pulmonary trunk is a left-sided mediastinal relation.
rationales.d: A generic ventricle is not the key right lung relation; SVC is the named vessel.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q013.takeaway: The right vagus nerve passes posterior to the root of the right lung and contributes to the pulmonary plexus.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q013.displayText:
The right vagus nerve passes posterior to the root of the right lung and contributes to the pulmonary plexus.

The vagus nerve is posterior to the root of the lung.

The roots of the lung are at the level of T5-T7 vertebral bodies. The phrenic nerve is anterior to the root of the lung.
emphasis: The right vagus nerve passes posterior to the root of the right lung and contributes to the pulmonary plexus

rationales.a: Right atrium lies anterior/inferior to the root rather than posterior.
rationales.c: SVC is anterior to the root.
rationales.d: Phrenic nerve passes anterior to the lung root.

marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q014.takeaway: The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung to join the superior vena cava.
marrow__ANAT_CH46_Q014.displayText:
The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung to join the superior vena cava.

The area marked 'A' is where the azygos vein arches over the hilum of the right lung.

The diagram shown is of the right lung, identified by the presence of hyparterial and eparterial bronchus at the hilum.
emphasis: The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung to join the superior vena cava

rationales.a: SVC is the recipient of the azygos arch rather than the vessel looping over the root.
rationales.b: The aortic arch is a left-sided structure.
rationales.d: Left brachiocephalic vein crosses anteriorly and is not the arch over the right hilum.
